title: RBAC v2: structured denial reason codes + optional authz debug header
author: Kaitlyn Nguyen
description: Problem: With RBAC v2 deny-by-default landing across Gateway + Control Plane, Support and Console UX need consistent, structured signals to answer “why was I denied?” without leaking policy internals or creating side-channel disclosure. Today we return a generic 403 from several stacks and each service/gateway path formats errors differently, making troubleshooting slow (and leading to tickets like SUP-48305/INT-19022). This PR introduces a shared set of denial reason codes and a gated, optional debug header mechanism for admin troubleshooting. Summary of changes: (1) Add canonical AuthzDenialReasonCode enum (and mapping helpers) in the shared authz package. (2) Standardize PermissionDenied error payload shape across gateway + control-plane HTTP handlers (no policy details; includes stable reason code + request id). (3) Add opt-in debug response headers behind BOTH a feature flag and an admin-only permission check, so authorized admins can see a high-level explanation in-flight without needing server logs. (4) Add metrics and logs to quantify deny reasons (for rollout dashboards) while keeping user-visible errors minimal. API/behavior details: - Default behavior (no debug): 403 with error code PERMISSION_DENIED and a structured denial_reason_code field (string) plus request_id; message remains generic ("permission denied"). - Debug behavior (admin-only): if request includes header X-Redwood-Debug-Authz: 1 AND caller has permission rbac.debug_authz AND rbac_debug_headers_enabled flag is on, then response includes headers: X-Redwood-Authz-Decision: deny|allow, X-Redwood-Authz-Reason: <reason_code>, X-Redwood-Authz-Required-Permission: <permission>, X-Redwood-Authz-Scope: <scope_type>:<scope_id>. We intentionally do not include the evaluated role names, bindings, group ids, or full policy graph. - For non-admins or when flag disabled: the request proceeds normally but debug headers are not included; we do not return a different error to avoid oracle behavior (we only log internally that a debug header was requested but suppressed). Denial reason codes included (initial set): - MISSING_PERMISSION (subject lacks required permission for action) - SCOPE_MISMATCH (permission exists but not for requested scope) - SUBJECT_UNRESOLVED (no subject / token mapping failed) - POLICY_VERSION_UNAVAILABLE (policy fetch failed / stale) - EVALUATION_TIMEOUT (authz evaluation exceeded budget) - BREAK_GLASS_REQUIRED (endpoint requires break-glass elevation) - ENDPOINT_UNANNOTATED (sensitive endpoint missing permission annotation; treated as deny in v2 mode) - FEATURE_FLAG_DISABLED (v2 enforcement / endpoint guard disabled; used internally for debug + metrics) Notes on info disclosure: Debug headers are only emitted for callers who already have rbac.debug_authz. This is designed for Org Admin/Security Admin flows in Console and for Support during guided troubleshooting with customer administrators. We also redact in Hosted multi-tenant environments by default (flag off), but enable in dedicated/private dogfood and pilot envs. Test coverage: unit tests for reason code mapping and redaction, gateway integration tests for header gating and consistent payload shape, and a control-plane handler test to validate ENDPOINT_UNANNOTATED denies when v2 enforcement is enabled. Follow-ups: Console “Why denied?” UX will consume denial_reason_code + request_id immediately; debug header view will be exposed only in admin troubleshooting pane (separate PR in console repo).

review_conversation: Marcus Lin (Security Eng): “I like the direction, but I’m worried about leaking required permissions/scope IDs to non-admins. Can we guarantee headers never show up unless the caller is explicitly privileged? Also please confirm we aren’t creating an oracle where requesting debug changes the response.” Kaitlyn Nguyen (author): “Yep. Debug headers require: (1) request header present, (2) rbac_debug_headers_enabled flag enabled, (3) allow decision by authz check for permission rbac.debug_authz. If any condition fails, we do not alter the response body/status; we only omit debug headers. Added test cases for ‘requested but suppressed’ paths.” Amara Diallo (Gateway): “Can we ensure header emission happens after authz evaluation and is consistent for streaming routes? Also standardize casing and prefix. Suggest we use X-Redwood-Authz-* only.” Kaitlyn: “Updated to only emit X-Redwood-Authz-* headers and moved header population into a shared helper called after evaluation. Streaming route path uses the same middleware; added regression coverage.” Chloe Martin (Console backend): “Console needs a stable denial_reason_code in the JSON body, not only headers. Please confirm that it’s always present on 403 in v2 mode and that codes are stable.” Kaitlyn: “Added denial_reason_code to the error body for PermissionDenied in both gateway and control-plane. Codes are treated as stable API surface (documented in internal doc; customer-facing doc later).” Felix Schneider (Console): “For ‘why denied?’ we also need request_id. Is that present for both gateway and service errors?” Kaitlyn: “Yes; both paths include request_id and we align with our existing request id propagation header. Added tests to ensure request_id is present.” Jordan Lee (Policy engine): “Reason code mapping: EVALUATION_TIMEOUT vs POLICY_VERSION_UNAVAILABLE. Make sure timeouts are not conflated with cache misses.” Kaitlyn: “Separated evaluation budget timeouts from policy fetch failures; the evaluator returns distinct error types now and mapping reflects that. Added unit tests for each mapping.” Requested changes were addressed (naming/prefix, oracle behavior, mapping correctness), then approvals were given.
approvals: Approved-by: Marcus Lin; Approved-by: Amara Diallo; Approved-by: Chloe Martin
release_notes: RBAC v2 permission denied responses now include a stable denial_reason_code and request_id for troubleshooting.
Admin-only, feature-flagged debug headers can be enabled for guided “why denied?” investigations without exposing policy internals.
